blocks.text: “I declare,” he says, “I declare most seriously that I almost feel my name has been stained. I shall feel this until this crime is solved and punished by law. This gentleman gave a large part of his life to serving me. This gentleman gave the last day of his life to serving me. This gentleman often ate at my table and slept under my roof. He leaves my house for his own, and within an hour he is struck down. He may have been followed from my house, or watched while he was there. He may even have first been chosen as a target because of his connection with my house. That connection may have made him seem richer and much more important. His own quiet manner would not have suggested such wealth or importance. I have money, influence, and a high position in society. If I cannot use these to uncover everyone responsible for this crime, I fail to show my respect for that gentleman's memory. I also fail to show my loyalty to someone who was always loyal to me.”

He makes this statement very seriously and with great emotion. He looks round the room as if speaking to a large gathering. Mr. Bucket watches him closely, with a serious expression. There might even be a little pity in that look, if it were not so bold to imagine such a thing.

“Today's ceremony,” continues Sir Leicester, “showed very clearly how much the finest people in the land respected my dead friend.” He stresses the word “friend”, for death removes all differences in social rank. “That ceremony has, I say, made my shock even greater at this most horrible and shamelessly bold crime. If my own brother had committed it, I would not save him from punishment.”
Mr. Bucket looks very serious. Volumnia says that the dead man was the most trustworthy and dearest person!
“You must feel his death as a loss, miss,” replies Mr. Bucket in a calming voice, “no doubt. He was the sort of man whose death would be a loss, I'm sure he was.”

Volumnia replies that she has a sensitive mind. She has firmly decided never to recover from this loss as long as she lives. Her nerves are ruined for ever, and she has no hope at all of smiling again. Meanwhile, she folds a letter into the shape of a three-cornered hat. It is for that impressive and rather frightening old general at Bath, and describes her sadness.
“It gives a delicate woman a shock,” says Mr. Bucket with sympathy, “but the feeling will pass.”

More than anything, Volumnia wants to know what is being done. Are they going to find that dreadful soldier guilty, or whatever they call it? Did he have any helpers in the crime, or whatever the law calls them? She asks many more innocent questions of the same kind.

“Well, you see, miss,” replies Mr. Bucket, moving his finger to help persuade her. He is so naturally charming towards women that he has almost called her “my dear”. “It isn't easy to answer those questions at this moment. Not at this moment. I've worked on this case, Sir Leicester Dedlock, Baronet, morning, noon, and night.” Mr. Bucket brings Sir Leicester into the conversation because of his importance. “Without a glass or two of sherry, I don't think I could have kept my mind working so hard. I could answer your questions, miss, but my duty won't allow it. Sir Leicester Dedlock, Baronet, will very soon hear everything we have discovered. And I hope he may find it”—Mr. Bucket looks serious again—“satisfactory.”

The weak and sickly cousin only hopes some fellow will be executed—to set an example. Thinks you need more influence these days—to get a man hanged—than to get a man a job paying ten thousand a year. Hasn't a doubt—set an example—far better to hang the wrong fellow than no fellow.
